opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, it's great to be here.

I think of them as deeply intertwined, but not the same thing. Drug design is ultimately an engineering problem: you're trying to create a molecule that does something very specific in the body. It binds the right target, avoids the wrong ones, gets to where it needs to go, and doesn't cause harm along the way. But you can't really engineer well in a system you don't understand. So modeling the biological world is the foundation, and drug design is what you build on top of it.

For a long time the field has been limited by how much of that biology we could actually see. Experimental methods for determining structures, measuring binding, or understanding how a protein moves are incredibly valuable, but they're slow and expensive, and they only cover a tiny fraction of the space we care about. What AI is starting to give us is the ability to model these systems computationally, with enough accuracy that we can trust the predictions and act on them. Structure prediction was a big moment for that. Suddenly you could see the shape of a protein, and increasingly how it interacts with other molecules, without waiting months for an experiment.

The way I like to frame it is that once you have good models of the biology, drug design becomes a search problem in a space you can actually explore. Instead of making thousands of molecules in the lab and hoping a few work, you can ask the models: if I change this part of the molecule, what happens to binding? What happens to selectivity? You run that loop in silico, very quickly, and only take the most promising ideas into the lab. The lab then tells you where your models were wrong, and that feeds back in.

So understanding the biology isn't a side quest on the way to drugs. It's the thing that makes rational design possible at all. And as these models get more general, covering not just one target or one chemistry but the whole range of molecular interactions, the hope is that drug design starts to look less like artisanal trial and error and more like a principled engineering discipline.

r001.rationale: The response describes computational biology models as tools for evaluating molecule changes in an in-silico search loop, but it does not propose using them as environments for AI agents to explore.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that drug design is really a downstream consequence of how well you can model biology. If you have a model that genuinely captures how proteins fold, how small molecules bind, how a perturbation to one part of a cell propagates through the rest of it, then designing a drug becomes a search problem over that model. You're asking: what molecule, if I introduce it into this system, moves the system into the state I want? That's a very natural thing for AI to do once the underlying model is good enough.

But the honest reality is that our models of biology are still very incomplete. We have pockets where they're remarkably good, structure prediction being the obvious one, and then huge areas where we're essentially in the dark. So a lot of what we're doing at Isomorphic is trying to expand those pockets. The exciting thing about AlphaFold 3 was that it moved from modeling proteins in isolation to modeling proteins with ligands, nucleic acids, ions, all the things that actually matter for whether a drug works. Each time you widen the scope of what the model can represent, you widen the set of design questions you can ask it.

The other piece is that these two things feed each other. When you design a molecule, make it, and test it, you learn something about where your model was wrong. That's data you'd never get from just passively observing nature. So I think of modeling and design as a loop rather than two separate activities: better models enable better design, and the act of designing generates exactly the kind of data that improves the models. The ambition is to run that loop fast enough and at enough scale that the model of biology keeps getting better and the drugs that fall out of it keep getting more reliable.

r001.rationale: The response describes drug design as searching over a model of biology, but does not propose using that model as an environment for AI agents to explore.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re deeply connected. To design a drug, you need to understand enough about the biological system to predict what will happen when you intervene in it. But biology is incredibly complex, so the question is: what do you need to model, and at what level of detail, to make a useful design decision?

A protein structure, for example, gives you a powerful piece of information, but it doesn’t tell you everything about how a molecule will interact with that protein, or what the downstream effect will be in a cell. You need to connect those different levels of understanding to the properties you’re trying to achieve in a drug.

And the relationship goes both ways. You build models that help you design molecules, then you make and test those molecules, and the experiments teach you something new about the biology. That feedback loop is really exciting: better models enable better experiments, and better experiments enable better models. You don’t have to solve all of biology before you can make progress on designing a drug.

r001.rationale: The response discusses modeling biology to support drug design and learn from experiments, but it does not propose using biochemical models as environments for AI agents to explore.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re deeply connected, but they’re not quite the same problem. Modeling biology is about understanding how a system behaves: how a protein interacts with another protein, how a cell responds to a perturbation. Designing a drug is about intervening in that system to produce a particular outcome.

The exciting thing about AI is that you can start to connect those two. If you have a model that can predict what happens when you change a molecule, you can use it to search for molecules with the properties you want. But that prediction has to be tested experimentally. The model proposes something, you measure what actually happens, and those results inform the next round of design.

So I see it as a loop between prediction, design, and experiment. You don’t necessarily need a complete simulation of biology to make a useful drug. You need models that capture the right aspects of biology well enough to help you make better decisions—and experiments that tell you where those models are wrong.

r001.rationale: The response describes models predicting molecular effects to guide drug search, but it does not propose using biochemical models as environments for AI agents to explore.
